newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan government brighter on land market.
newsitem.headline: Japan government brighter on land market.

text.p: Japan's land prices are almost stable after years of declines, the government said on Friday, brightening its assessment of one of the most closely watched areas of the economy.

But the government's National Land Agency disappointed some stock punters who on Thursday pushed up property related shares in expectations of an official declaration that residential land prices had bottomed out.
"Prices of residential land in major cities have almost stabilised, and commercial land prices have also calmed down greatly," Land Agency Minister Kosuke Ito told reporters.
He said it was the first time land prices had shown signs of stabilising since they plummeted with the bursting of the "bubble economy" of inflated asset prices in the early 1990s.
Japanese land prices fell for a sixth straight year in 1996, with commercial land prices in central Tokyo down 70 percent from their peak in 1991.
An agency official said, however, that while residential land prices were flattening out, they had not completely bottomed out.
He added that there were still some residential areas in Tokyo that showed some price declines in the January to March quarter.

A survey by the Land Institute of Japan, a government affiliated research body, showed that in the greater Tokyo area residential land prices declined 0.7 percent, while commercial land prices slipped 2.8 percent.
Property-related shares fell back on Friday but analysts said the fall was more likely to due to profit-taking than any real dashing of expectations.
They said they were bullish on large property firms and criticised the government's assessment as based on lagging indicators and being behind the curve.
"Commercial land prices bottomed out this year," said Juniichi Shiomoto, a real estate analyst at Nomura Research Institute.
But he was more cautious about residential prices, which he said could fall again if interest rates rose and discouraged condominium builders.
Analysts said there was a growing distinction between attractive large land plots and those which were not big enough to build buildings, adding that firms with good portfolios were good buys.
They singled out companies such as Mitsubishi Estate Co Ltd and Sumitomo Realty and Development Co Ltd and Mitsui Fudosan Co Ltd.

Mitsubishi Estate and Sumitomo Realty showed steep falls in earnings for the past business year, while Mitsui Fudosan posted a loss. But all three have forecast better earnings for this business year.
"I think we could say that the worst is over. We have already hit bottom," said a Mitsubishi Estate spokesman.
